questions.problem:
Suppose we take a random sample of size $n=80$ from a population where $42%$ of the population has a particular characteristic. Find a normal approximation for the probability that more than $35%$ of the sample has the characteristic. You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ are given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.*

| $z$ | $\,0.05\,$ | $\,0.06\,$ | $\,0.07\,$ | $\,0.08\,$ | $\,0.09\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,-1.4\,$ | $\,0.0735\,$ | $\,0.0721\,$ | $\,0.0708\,$ | $\,0.0694\,$ | $\,0.0681\,$ |
| $\,-1.3\,$ | $\,0.0885\,$ | $\,0.0869\,$ | $\,0.0853\,$ | $\,0.0838\,$ | $\,0.0823\,$ |
| $\,-1.2\,$ | $\,0.1056\,$ | $\,0.1038\,$ | $\,0.1020\,$ | $\,0.1003\,$ | $\,0.0985\,$ |
questions.worked_solution:
Given a population in which a proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic, the sampling distribution of the sample proportion $\overset{^}{\,p}$ can be approximated as

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}),
$$

where the sample size $n$ is much smaller than the population size, $np>5,$ and $n(1-p)>5.$

In our case

- the sample size is $n=80,$ and

- the population proportion is $p=0.42.$

Now, since

$$
np=80(0.42)=33.6>5
$$

and

$$
n(1-p)=80(1-0.42)=46.4>5,
$$

and $n=80$ is much smaller than the population size, we can apply the above approximation.

The sampling distribution of the sample proportion, in this case, can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{^}{\,p} & ∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}) \\  & ∼N(0.42,\frac{0.42(1-0.42)}{80}) \\  & ∼N(0.42,0.003\,045).\end{aligned}
$$

The probability we wish to find is
$P(\overset{^}{\,p}>0.35).$
So, we convert $\overset{^}{\,p}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{^}{\,p}>0.35) & =P(Z>\frac{0.35-0.42}{\sqrt{0.003\,045}}) \\  & ≈P(Z>-1.27) \\  & =1-P(Z<-1.27) \\  & =1-Φ(-1.27).\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-1.27) & =0.1020.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{^}{\,p}>0.35) & =1-Φ(-1.27) \\  & =1-0.1020 \\  & =0.8980.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
For which of the following situations can the distribution of the sample proportion $\overset{^}{\,p}$ be approximated as

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}),
$$

where $p$ is the population proportion?

I. A sample of $50$ students from a class, where $60%$ of the students in the school have an IQ greater than $105.$

II. A sample of $60$ paid TV customers, where $80%$ of the customers watch TV more than $8$ hours per week.

III. A sample of $40$ players in a team, $90%$ of the players in the league are right-handed.

*Hint: In each case, you may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.*
questions.worked_solution:
Given a population in which a proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic, the sampling distribution of the sample proportion $\overset{^}{\,p}$ can be approximated as

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}),
$$

where 

- $n\le 5%\cdot N$ (the sample size is less than (or equal to) $5%$ of the population size),

- $np>5$ (more than $5$ sample elements have the characteristic), and

- $n(1-p)>5$ (more than $5$ sample elements do not have the characteristic).

We're given that the population is significantly larger than the sample size in each case. Therefore, we may assume that the first condition is satisfied in each case.

Let's now examine each situation.

- In situation I, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}np & =50(0.6) \\  & =30 \\  & >5\,✓ \\ n(1-p) & =50(1-0.6) \\  & =20 \\  & >5.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can approximate the distribution of $\overset{^}{\,p}$ using the given model.

- In situation II, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}np & =60(0.8) \\  & =48 \\  & >5\,✓ \\ n(1-p) & =60(1-0.8) \\  & =12 \\  & >5.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can approximate the distribution of $\overset{^}{\,p}$ using the given model.

- In situation III, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}np & =40(0.9) \\  & =36 \\  & >5\,✓ \\ n(1-p) & =40(1-0.9) \\  & =4 \\  & ≯5.\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Since $n(1-p)≯5,$ we *cannot* approximate the distribution of $\overset{^}{\,p}$ using the given model.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

questions.problem:
A call center manager knows that $40%$ of the calls are complaints. If the manager randomly samples $80$ calls, find a normal approximation for the probability that more than $32$ but fewer than $36$ of them are complaints. You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.

*Note: $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.*
questions.worked_solution:
Given a population in which a proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic, the sampling distribution of the sample proportion $\overset{^}{\,p}$ can be approximated as

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}),
$$

where the sample size $n$ is much smaller than the population size, $np>5,$ and $n(1-p)>5.$

In our case

- the sample size is $n=80,$ and

- the population proportion is $p=0.4.$

Now, since

$$
np=80(0.4)=32>5
$$

and

$$
n(1-p)=80(1-0.4)=48>5,
$$

and $n=80$ is much smaller than the population size, we can apply the above approximation.

The sampling distribution of the sample proportion, in this case, can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{^}{\,p} & ∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}) \\  & ∼N(0.4,\frac{0.4(1-0.4)}{80}) \\  & ∼N(0.4,0.0030).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we determine the probability we wish to find. If more than $32$ but fewer than $36$ calls are complaints, then 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{32}{80}<\overset{^}{\,p} & <\frac{36}{80} \\ 0.4\le \overset{^}{\,p} & \le 0.45.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the probability we wish to find is
$P(0.4<\overset{^}{\,p}<0.45).$
So, we convert $\overset{^}{\,p}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0.4\le \overset{^}{\,p}\le 0.45) & =P(\frac{0.4-0.4}{\sqrt{0.0030}}<Z<\frac{0.45-0.4}{\sqrt{0.0030}}) \\  & ≈P(0<Z<0.91) \\  & =P(Z<0.91)-P(Z<0.00) \\  & =Φ(0.91)-Φ(0.00)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0.4<\overset{^}{\,p}<0.45) & =Φ(0.91)-Φ(0).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
A newspaper in a town has $100\,000$ subscribers, and $56\,000$ of them have a digital subscription. If the newspaper randomly samples $224$ subscribers, find a normal approximation for the probability that between $112$ and $140$ subscribers (inclusive) in the sample have a digital subscription. You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size. *Hint: Two tables of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ are given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *
$z$$\,0.00\,$$\,0.01\,$$\,0.02\,$
$\,-1.8\,$ $\,0.0359\,$ $\,0.0351\,$ $\,0.0344\,$
$\,-1.7\,$ $\,0.0446\,$ $\,0.0436\,$ $\,0.0427\,$
$\,-1.6\,$ $\,0.0548\,$ $\,0.0537\,$ $\,0.0526\,$
$z$$\,0.05\,$$\,0.06\,$$\,0.07\,$
$\,1.7\,$ $\,0.9599\,$ $\,0.9608\,$ $\,0.9616\,$
$\,1.8\,$ $\,0.9678\,$ $\,0.9686\,$ $\,0.9693\,$
$\,1.9\,$ $\,0.9744\,$ $\,0.9750\,$ $\,0.9756\,$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a population in which a proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic, the sampling distribution of the sample proportion $\overset{^}{\,p}$ can be approximated as

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}),
$$

where the sample size $n$ is much smaller than the population size, $np>5,$ and $n(1-p)>5.$

In our case

- the sample size is $n=224,$ and

- the population proportion is $p=\frac{56\,000}{100\,000}=0.56.$

Now, since

$$
np=224(0.56)=125.44>5
$$

and

$$
n(1-p)=224(1-0.56)=98.56>5,
$$

and the $n=224$ is much smaller than the population size, we can apply the above approximation.

The sampling distribution of the sample proportion, in this case, can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{^}{\,p} & ∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}) \\  & ∼N(0.56,\frac{0.56(1-0.56)}{224}) \\  & ∼N(0.56,0.0011).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we determine the probability we wish to find. If between $112$ and $140$ of subscribers in the sample have a digital subscription, then

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{112}{224}\le \overset{^}{\,p} & \le \frac{140}{224} \\ 0.5\le \overset{^}{\,p} & \le 0.625.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the probability we wish to find is
$P(0.5\le \overset{^}{\,p}\le 0.625).$
So, we convert $\overset{^}{\,p}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0.5\le \overset{^}{\,p}\le 0.625) & =P(\frac{0.5-0.56}{\sqrt{0.0011}}\le Z\le \frac{0.625-0.56}{\sqrt{0.0011}}) \\  & ≈P(-1.81\le Z\le 1.96) \\  & =P(Z\le 1.96)-P(Z\le -1.81) \\  & =Φ(1.96)-Φ(-1.81)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(1.96)=0.9750,\,Φ(-1.81)=0.0351.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0.5\le \overset{^}{\,p}\le 0.625) & =Φ(1.96)-Φ(-1.81) \\  & =0.9750-0.0351 \\  & =0.9399.\end{aligned}
$$
